questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t-4)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+3)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t$ can take any real value.
What is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Used $t=x-4$ instead of $t=x+4$ when making $t$ the subject.
Replaced $t$ by $x$ directly instead of by $x+4$.
Substituted into $2t$ correctly but dropped the $+3$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t+3)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}-1)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t$ can take any real value.
What is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Used $t=x+3$ instead of $t=x-3$, giving $(x+3)^{2}$.
Added $1$ instead of subtracting it at the end, giving $9+1$ rather than $9-1$.
Used $t=x+3$ and also added $1$ instead of subtracting it.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=7\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+7\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$.
What is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Used the radius itself instead of the square of the radius.
Used $\cos^{2}t-\sin^{2}t$ rather than the identity $\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t=1$.
Used a difference of squares and the radius rather than its square.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}+2)\underset{\sim}{i}+4t^{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t$ can take any real value.
Which fully describes its path?

options.why: Gave the full line and ignored that $x=t^{2}+2$ can never be less than $2$.
Substituted $t^{2}=x+2$ instead of $t^{2}=x-2$.
Substituted $t^{2}=x+2$ and also gave the full line instead of the ray.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2-3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Which best describes its path?

options.why: Ignored the restriction $t\ge0$, which stops the path at its starting point.
Used the coefficients of $t$ as the starting point instead of the constant terms.
Used the coefficients of $t$ as the starting point and ignored the restriction $t\ge0$.

questions.solution_text:
Both components are linear in $t$, so the path lies on a straight line.
At $t=0$ the particle is at $(2,1)$.
Since $t\ge0$, the particle never goes back past $(2,1)$, so the path is a ray starting at $(2,1)$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(4t-1)\underset{\sim}{i}+(6t+5)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t$ can take any real value.
What is the Cartesian equation of its path?

options.why: Used $t=\frac{x-1}{4}$ instead of $t=\frac{x+1}{4}$.
Inverted the ratio of the coefficients, using $\frac{4}{6}$ in place of $\frac{6}{4}$.
Inverted the ratio of the coefficients and used $t=\frac{x-1}{4}$.

questions.question_text:
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3t\underset{\sim}{i}+t^{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge0$.
Which fully describes its path?

options.why: Gave the whole parabola, ignoring that $x=3t\ge0$.
Divided by $3$ once instead of squaring $\frac{x}{3}$.
Divided by $3$ once instead of squaring, and gave the whole parabola.

questions.question_text:
A particle travels once anticlockwise around the circle $(x-1)^{2}+(y+4)^{2}=25$, starting at $(6,-4)$.
Which position vector function describes this motion for $0\le t\le2\pi$?

options.why: Read the centre's $y$-coordinate as $4$ rather than $-4$ from $(y+4)^{2}$.
Used $25$ as the radius instead of taking the square root to get $5$.
Used $25$ as the radius and read the centre's $y$-coordinate as $4$.

questions.solution_text:
The circle has centre $(1,-4)$ and radius $\sqrt{25}=5$.
$x=1+5\cos t$
$y=-4+5\sin t$
At $t=0$ this gives $(1+5,-4)=(6,-4)$, the required starting point.
$\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(1+5\cos t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(5\sin t-4)\underset{\sim}{j}$
